title: What is known about 1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA0RF_---1RE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA0RF_---1RE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and looks out of reach. A block of 1s grows by two each sweep; behind it a chaotic counter eats a reservoir. An exact accelerated simulation followed the machine to the moment the counter reached the far end, the first point since sweep 91 where it could halt: at step 8,423,661,719,239,282,477 the whole block (3,351,350,288 ones) became a new reservoir instead. The next such moment is of the order of 2300,000,000 sweeps away. In scaled-down models about one contact in three ends in a halt, so the machine probably halts, but nobody can say when.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,694 cells have been visited and 24,088 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The sweep map ignores the block
claims.text: At each visit of the left end in state D the tape is D>0 1^n R. memosim keeps 8 block cells and R and counts the rest of the block by formula; in check mode its block, R and step count agree with the direct run at each of 20,000 visits (0 mismatches).

claims.title: No halt in the first 8.42·10<sup>18</sup> steps; the sixth event
claims.text: Events (the head comes home in state C and the block becomes a reservoir) happen after visits 3, 5, 7, 15, 91 and 1,675,675,235. At the last one the block is 13,351,350,288, the head leaves the region at step 8,423,661,719,239,282,477, and the next visit (block of 2) is at step 8,423,661,722,590,632,760 with a region of 3,351,350,501 cells: 1,675,675,146 pairs 01 and a 209-cell tail. The run gives the same event with memo widths 30 and 52 (the table only skips work, entries come from the cell-by-cell run); widths 0 to 52 agree at 3·106 visits.

claims.title: Next event about 2<sup>3·10^8</sup> sweeps away
claims.text: From a fresh reservoir the deepest cell reached advances 6.5 to 11 cells per doubling of the number of sweeps, and the new reservoir has 3.35·10<sup>9</sup> cells.

claims.title: In short-block models, contacts halt about one time in three
claims.text: The real machine with the block cut back to 4 cells at every visit, from random regions: all of 2,000 runs (8 pairs) halt within 6 events and all of 500 (16 pairs) within 11, always with blank tape right of the head. With the last 41 cells of the true tail at the far end, 132 of 400 runs halt at the first contact.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: The head sweeps across the whole tape and adds two cells per sweep at the left end, so the tape grows like the square root of the step count.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Not proved either: that a halt can only happen at the far end (the parity-window tape language that proves it for the sibling ..._1RA1RF_---1RD is not closed enough here: it allows halts inside the tape for windows up to 10 cells).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and it may stay that way. A block of ones grows at every sweep; behind it a scrambled counter slowly eats a reservoir. Only when the reservoir is used up can the machine stop, and each time that moment has passed, the next one is unimaginably further away. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the pieces.

facts.text: No halt: an exact accelerated run to the sixth event, where a block of 3.35·10<sup>9</sup> ones became the new reservoir.
Estimated wait for the next moment at which it could halt.
Share of far-end contacts that halt in scaled-down models of the machine.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: A growing block, a busy counter, a reservoir
html: Look at the tape each time the head reaches the left end. It always has the same parts: a block of ones that is two cells longer than last time; a short busy stretch that changes from sweep to sweep; a long regular reservoir of pairs 01; and a short tail left over from earlier times.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 70" role="img" aria-label="The tape: a growing uniform block, an active counter region, a reservoir it eats, and an old tail at the far end" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="10" y="14">← grows 2 cells a sweep</text><text x="14" y="60">growing block</text><text x="184" y="60">busy counter</text><text x="274" y="60">reservoir</text><text x="484" y="60">old tail</text></g><rect x="10" y="20" width="170" height="22" fill="var(--ink)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="180" y="20" width="90" height="22" fill="var(--heur-bg)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="270" y="20" width="210" height="22" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="480" y="20" width="90" height="22" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/></svg>

Crossing the block costs time but changes nothing: what the head does behind the block does not depend on how long the block is. So the machine applies one fixed rule, sweep after sweep, to the part of the tape behind the block. That is what makes it possible to simulate 1018 steps: a program can keep the part behind the block, forget the block, and add up the steps by formula.

sections.heading: A counter with no digits
html: The busy stretch behaves like an odometer: cells next to the block change at almost every sweep, deeper cells more and more rarely, and the deepest cell ever touched moves into the reservoir by a few cells each time the number of sweeps doubles. But unlike an odometer it has no separate digits that could be read off and predicted: how deep a sweep goes looks like a run of coin tosses. That is why the only way found to know what it does is to run it.

When the counter reaches the far end, the head comes home in a different state and turns the whole block into a fresh reservoir (an event); a new block starts from two cells. This happened after sweeps 3, 5, 7, 15 and 91, and then not again for a long time: the 209-cell region of sweep 92 lasted until sweep 1,675,675,235, about 8.42·1018 steps in.

sections.heading: A coin toss, repeated at ever longer intervals
html: Between two events nothing can go wrong: the machine sweeps, the block grows, the counter eats a little more reservoir. Everything is decided in the few sweeps in which the counter touches the far end of the tape. Each such contact either stops the machine or turns the block into the next reservoir, which is as long as the block had become, so the next contact is exponentially further away than the last one, and the one after that exponentially further again.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 96" role="img" aria-label="Epochs: each reservoir is as long as the block was at the previous event, so each epoch is exponentially longer than the one before" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="10" y="14">epoch k: reservoir of L cells</text><text x="10" y="58">epoch k+1: reservoir of about 2^(L/c) cells</text><text x="300" y="36">eaten in about 2^(L/c) sweeps</text></g><rect x="10" y="20" width="60" height="18" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="70" y="20" width="14" height="18" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="10" y="64" width="520" height="18" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="530" y="64" width="14" height="18" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><circle cx="84" cy="29" r="4" fill="var(--head)"/><circle cx="544" cy="73" r="4" fill="var(--head)"/></svg>

Machines like this are called cryptids in the Busy Beaver community: their fate hangs on an unbounded sequence of yes/no questions about a pseudo-random process, and no known method answers all of them at once.

For this machine the last contact was simulated exactly: no halt. To guess the odds of the following ones, one can shrink the machine: keep the block at four cells, so that reservoirs stay short and contacts come quickly. From thousands of random starting regions, every such run eventually halts, always at the blank far end of the tape, and about a third of the contacts are fatal. If the real contacts are like that, the machine halts with probability 1, but the expected waiting time is a tower of exponentials.

sections.heading: What was checked, and how
html:
• The accelerated simulator (memosim) reproduces the block length, the region and the exact step count of the real machine at each of 20,000 consecutive sweeps.
  • Its shortcut table can be made wider, narrower or switched off without changing the run; two widths were run all the way to the event and agree on the sweep, the tape and the step.
  • An independent earlier program found the same event sweep.
  • Not proved: that the machine cannot halt in the middle of the tape. It has never been seen to, in the real run or in any model run.

family: chaotic counter eating a reservoir (cryptid-like; events at far-end contacts)
summary: A chaotic counter eats a reservoir behind a growing block; an exact accelerated run passes the sixth far-end contact at step 8.42e18 without a halt (new reservoir 3.35e9 cells), the next contact is about 2^(3e8) sweeps away, and in short-block models about a third of contacts halt.
